cases.answer: A window resize event only fires when the viewport changes. A sidebar collapsing or a web font loading can resize a card while the window stays the same size. ResizeObserver reports that element's own size change.

cases.answer: If teams release on their own schedules and the shared parts are stable, I'd publish a versioned package with semantic versioning, changelogs and a deprecation policy, so each team upgrades when it is ready. If the teams are tightly coupled and change things together, a monorepo makes atomic changes easier, but it needs clear ownership and CI that only runs the affected suites.
should() re-runs the query and its assertion until it passes or times out. A then() callback runs one time, and an assertion in it can read the page before it has updated.
Use ResizeObserver because it is faster than a window resize listener and fires before the browser paints anything.
cases.notes: Keyword present, but the stated cause (speed) is not why ResizeObserver is used; the real reason (element vs viewport size) is absent.

cases.answer: Implicit wait is a global timeout that applies to every findElement call. Explicit wait uses WebDriverWait with a condition, like waiting until a button is clickable, and that's what I'd normally use. Fluent wait is an explicit wait where you also set the polling interval and which exceptions to ignore. I wouldn't mix implicit and explicit waits.
cases.notes: Covers all three plus the mixing guidance. 'When each is appropriate' is implied by 'what I'd normally use'.

cases.answer: Implicit wait is the best choice because it waits for every condition, including clickability, across the whole suite. Explicit waits are basically Thread.sleep with a fixed time. Fluent wait is only for mobile tests. You should combine implicit and explicit waits so the timeouts add up predictably.
